slides.title: The Single Point of Failure Problem
slides.body:
Single Point Failure
Subheading: The Core Problem
A web application running on one server has only one path for every request. If that server fails, the whole application stops — this is the single-point-of-failure problem. Cloud architectures solve it by placing more than one backend server behind a traffic distributor.
A single point of failure is one component whose failure alone stops the entire application from working.
Hardware failure, an operating-system patch, or a crash removes the only server handling requests.
Traffic above that one server's capacity slows or drops requests, with no second server to absorb the load.
Replacing the lone server with a bigger one raises the ceiling but never removes the single point of failure.
Analogy: A railway station with only one ticket counter forces every passenger to wait once that counter closes for a break — exactly as a single server failing removes the only route available for every user's request.
Visual Guidance: Left: one browser icon with an arrow into one server box, a red cross through it. Right: the same browser with arrows into two server boxes, one still green.
slides.notes: Open by stating plainly that one server means one failure point, tying it to the earlier horizontal-scaling idea from networking. Use the ticket-counter picture to make the outage feel concrete before naming load balancing. An interviewer may ask what single point of failure means in a web architecture — this slide is that answer.

slides.title: What a Load Balancer Does
slides.body:
Traffic Distribution
Subheading: Load Balancer Role
A load balancer sits in front of a group of backend servers and routes each incoming request to one of them, so no single server is a mandatory stop for every user.
Running identical servers behind the load balancer lets one fail without stopping the application for users.
Adding or removing backend servers behind the load balancer changes total capacity without changing application code.
Amazon Web Services offers this as the Elastic Load Balancing service, set up from the EC2 console's Load Balancers page.
An Application Load Balancer is billed for every hour it runs, plus the traffic it processes.
Choosing a load balancer type is therefore a cost decision, not only a technical one.
Visual Guidance: One load-balancer icon in the middle, arrows fanning out to three server icons below it; label the top arrow 'incoming requests'.
slides.notes: Explain the load balancer as the layer that stands between users and servers, deciding where each request goes. Point out that this is the exact service used later in the practical, reachable from the EC2 console. A common interview question is why a fixed server address cannot be handed to users directly — this mechanism is the answer.

slides.title: Purpose: Availability and Scalability
slides.body:
Availability Scalability Goals
Subheading: Why It Exists
Removing the single point of failure is not the only gain: the same routing that steers traffic away from a failed server also lets capacity grow simply by adding more servers behind it.
Availability: traffic keeps reaching healthy servers even while one instance fails or is being patched.
Scalability: new servers can join behind the load balancer as demand grows, without any downtime for users.
Horizontal scaling works safely only when the load balancer, not a fixed server address, is what users actually reach.
Running extra backend servers for availability adds compute cost, a trade-off revisited later under cost optimisation.
Visual Guidance: Simple timeline: two servers growing to four behind the same load balancer icon, with a small cost-tag icon beside the fourth server.
slides.notes: Stress that availability and scalability come from the same mechanism — rerouting traffic — just applied to failure versus growth. Mention briefly that more servers mean more cost, without turning it into a pricing discussion. Close by noting that dividing traffic sensibly among several servers needs a defined distribution method, which the next section builds on.

slides.title: Load Balancer Types Overview
slides.body:
Load Balancer Types
Subheading: Two Classification Axes
Load balancers are classified along two independent questions: which network layer they read, and who is allowed to reach them. Both choices change routing intelligence, speed, and exposure.
The layer axis separates Layer 4 (transport) balancers from Layer 7 (application) balancers.
The exposure axis separates internet-facing balancers from internal, private-only balancers.
A real deployment combines one choice from each axis, such as an internet-facing Layer 7 balancer.
Visual Guidance: 2x2 grid: rows Layer 4 / Layer 7, columns Internet-facing / Internal, each cell naming a typical use case.
slides.notes: Set up both axes before going deep into either one. Say plainly: layer decides how smart the routing is, exposure decides who can send traffic. Mention this map will be filled in across the next three slides.

slides.title: Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Balancing
slides.body:
Transport Vs Application
Subheading: Balancer Comparison
A Layer 4 balancer reads only transport-layer headers and forwards packets without opening the request. A Layer 7 balancer terminates the connection and reads the full HTTP request before routing it. Amazon Web Services calls these the Network Load Balancer (NLB) and the Application Load Balancer (ALB).
Visual Guidance: Side-by-side packet diagrams: Layer 4 arrow passing through unopened; Layer 7 arrow opened to show HTTP headers before forwarding.
slides.notes: Emphasise the trade-off: Layer 4 is faster because it never opens the packet, Layer 7 is smarter because it does. Point at the AWS service names since they are what appears on the console. Interview hook: ask when NLB is preferred over ALB (raw TCP/UDP speed, preserving client IP).
tables: Reads full HTTP request and response
Rule-based routing to different pools by path or host

slides.title: Internal vs Internet-Facing
slides.body:
Internal Vs Internet-Facing
Subheading: Who Can Reach It
Every load balancer is also classified by exposure: an internet-facing balancer gets a public IP address and accepts traffic from the public internet, while an internal balancer gets only a private IP address, reachable solely from inside its own Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).
Internal balancers sit between internal tiers, such as an application tier calling a backend service.
Internal balancers shrink the attack surface because no public route to them ever exists.
Both exposure types can be built as Layer 4 or Layer 7, since the two axes are independent.
Analogy: An office building has a public reception desk anyone off the street can walk into, and separate staff-only corridors reachable only by employees already inside — just as an internet-facing balancer accepts any public visitor while an internal balancer accepts only traffic that already originates inside the VPC.
Visual Guidance: Diagram: public internet arrow hitting an internet-facing balancer icon with a public IP; a second balancer icon inside the VPC boundary with only internal arrows reaching it.
slides.notes: Stress that exposure is a separate decision from layer, not a variant of it. Give the everyday phrasing: public reception versus staff-only corridor. Point out that a microservice calling another microservice should never need a public-facing balancer. Exam hook: ask why placing a database-facing balancer internal-only is good security practice.

slides.title: Choosing Load Balancer Type
slides.body:
Choosing Balancer Type
Subheading: Combining Both Axes
Connecting the two axes, an architecture typically places an internet-facing Layer 7 balancer in front of user traffic, and an internal Layer 4 or Layer 7 balancer between internal services, so each hop only pays for the intelligence it actually needs before any request reaches a specific server.
AWS offers an Application Load Balancer (ALB) for Layer 7 traffic and a Network Load Balancer (NLB) for Layer 4 traffic.
The internet-facing or internal scheme is chosen once, when the load balancer is created in the EC2 console.
Public-facing websites typically use an internet-facing ALB; service-to-service calls typically use an internal NLB or ALB.
Visual Guidance: Architecture diagram: public internet to internet-facing ALB, ALB fans to a service tier, service tier to an internal NLB, internal NLB fans to a database tier.
slides.notes: Tie the two axes together with one concrete architecture so the choice feels practical, not abstract. Point at the EC2 console's load balancer creation screen as the actual place this setting lives. Note this sets up the next topic: once traffic reaches the right balancer type, an algorithm still decides which specific server gets each request.

slides.title: Distribution Algorithms Landscape
slides.body:
Distribution Algorithms
Subheading: Four Approaches Compared
A load balancer needs a rule to pick which healthy target serves each request, and the right rule depends on how traffic and server capacity vary. Production systems keep several such rules available side by side rather than relying on just one.
Round robin cycles through targets in fixed order, assuming every target can handle equal load.
Least connections picks the target with fewest active requests, adapting to real-time load.
IP hash maps a client's address to the same target every time, for session continuity.
Weighted distribution biases any of the above toward stronger targets using assigned capacity weights.
Visual Guidance: Four-quadrant diagram: load balancer in the centre, one arrow style per algorithm (cyclic, counter-based, hash-based, weighted) fanning out to target icons.
slides.notes: Frame this as the rulebook a load balancer consults for every single request. Stress that none of the four is universally best; each suits a different traffic shape. An interviewer may ask which algorithm fits a given scenario, so link each name to its one-line trigger.

slides.title: Round Robin And Weighting Mechanism
slides.body:
Round Robin Weighting
Subheading: Static Capacity Bias
Plain round robin treats every target as equal, which fails once servers differ in capacity. Weighted distribution corrects this by giving stronger targets a proportionally larger share of the fixed rotation.
Smooth weighted round robin increases each target's running total by its weight every pick, avoiding bursts to one server.
A 3:1 weight ratio still averages three requests to one target for every single request to the other, over time.
AWS Application Load Balancer target groups default to round robin, and support weighted target groups for traffic shifting.
Weights are set once from known capacity and do not change automatically with real-time load.
Visual Guidance: Sequence strip showing a weighted rotation order (e.g. A A A B) under two server icons sized differently to show capacity.
slides.notes: Explain smoothing with the running-total idea so the order does not look clumped, since that is a common exam trip-up. Point out that weights are a manual, planned setting, unlike least connections which reacts automatically. Mention the AWS target group weight field as the real-world location.

slides.title: Least Connections In Depth
slides.body:
Least Connections Depth
Subheading: Dynamic Load Tracking
Round robin and weighting both follow a fixed plan regardless of what is actually happening on each server. Least connections instead reacts continuously, sending each new request to whichever target is least busy right now.
The load balancer increments a per-target counter when a request starts and decrements it on completion.
Long-lived connections, like streaming or uploads, make this algorithm outperform round robin under uneven request durations.
AWS Application Load Balancer offers a least outstanding requests option, counting in-flight requests rather than raw connections.
The counter resets to zero whenever a target is marked unhealthy and removed from rotation temporarily.
Visual Guidance: Two target icons with live counters (e.g. 2 and 5) and an arrow from the load balancer pointing to the lower counter.
slides.notes: Emphasise the word 'live' — this counter updates on every request start and finish, unlike a weight set once in advance. Use an upload scenario to show why duration matters more than request count here. The AWS option name, least outstanding requests, is a common interview detail.

slides.title: IP Hash For Client Affinity
slides.body:
IP Hash Explained
Subheading: Client To Server Mapping
Some applications keep per-client state only on the server that first handled a request, so later requests from that client must reach the same target. IP hash solves this by hashing the client's source IP address to pick a target, keeping the mapping fixed while the target pool stays unchanged.
Adding or removing a target reshuffles the hash mapping, which can redirect many existing clients at once.
Clients sharing one corporate or mobile-network gateway IP can overload a single target disproportionately.
AWS Network Load Balancer uses flow hashing on IP and port for a similar effect at the transport layer.
This method needs no shared session store, unlike approaches that replicate session data across servers.
Analogy: A customer calling a company support line is always connected to the same agent because the caller ID is matched to an assignment list — just as IP hash always routes the same client IP to the same backend target based on the hash of its address.
Visual Guidance: Three client icons with distinct IPs, each with a dashed line always landing on the same one of two target icons, labelled 'hash(IP)'.
slides.notes: Open with the session-affinity problem before naming the term, per the teach-before-naming approach. Point out the reshuffle risk when a target is added or removed, since that is the usual follow-up interview question. Mention Network Load Balancer flow hashing as the transport-layer cousin of this idea.

slides.title: Comparing The Four Algorithms
slides.body:
Algorithms Compared
Subheading: Choosing The Right Fit
Each algorithm trades simplicity for adaptiveness differently, which is why production target groups often default to one while allowing an override for special cases.
Whichever algorithm a target group uses, it only sends traffic to targets that health checks have confirmed healthy.
Visual Guidance: Four-column table as the main visual; a small health-check icon beside the closing line to bridge forward.
slides.notes: Walk the table row by row, pairing each decision basis with its trade-off rather than re-reading the earlier slides. Use the closing line to set up that distribution never overrides a health check's verdict. A common interview ask is 'which algorithm for session-heavy apps' — point to IP hash's row.

slides.title: Health Checks And Session Handling Map
slides.body:
Health And Sessions
Subheading: Section Topic Map
A load balancer must know which backends are actually working, and decide how a user's follow-up requests are handled across multiple servers. Three linked questions cover this.
Health checks rely on configurable signals: how often to test and how long to wait for a reply.
A separate pair of thresholds decides how many consecutive passes or failures flip the health status.
Draining protects requests already underway by giving a failing or retiring backend a fixed grace window before full removal.
Session handling decides whether a returning user must reach the same backend again or any healthy one can serve them.
Visual Guidance: Three labelled boxes in a row: Health Checks, Draining, Sessions — each with a one-icon hint (heartbeat, tap closing, cookie).
slides.notes: Set up these three as one connected story: a load balancer first detects a problem, then removes the backend safely, and separately decides how to handle returning users. Mention this builds directly on the distribution algorithms already covered. Exam angle: expect a question distinguishing health checks from session stickiness, since both affect which server gets a request.

slides.title: Designing A Health Check
slides.body:
Health Check Design
Subheading: How Checks Work
A health check works like a repeated vitals check: the load balancer sends a small test request to each backend and reads the reply, confirming the application itself is responding, not just that the machine is switched on.
Interval sets how often the check repeats, for example every few seconds.
Timeout caps how long the backend has to reply before that attempt is counted as a miss.
The healthy threshold is the count of consecutive passes needed before traffic resumes to that backend.
The unhealthy threshold is the count of consecutive failures needed before traffic stops going to it.
Analogy: A doctor does not assume a patient is fine just because they are breathing; a short, repeated vitals check confirms the body is actually functioning — just as a health check confirms the server is actually serving requests correctly, not merely running.
Visual Guidance: Timeline strip showing repeated check pulses at fixed intervals, with a counter of consecutive passes/fails building toward the two thresholds.
slides.notes: Stress that a server can be powered on and still fail a health check, for instance if the application crashed while the operating system stays up. Use the everyday phrase 'repeated vitals check' before naming the thresholds. Interview hook: ask what happens if the interval is too long versus too short, since that trades detection speed against false alarms.

slides.title: Draining An Unhealthy Backend
slides.body:
Connection Draining
Subheading: Removing A Backend Safely
Removing a backend the instant it fails a check would cut off requests already mid-flight. Draining gives it a short grace period, called the deregistration delay, to finish current work before it fully leaves rotation.
New requests stop being sent to the backend as soon as it is marked unhealthy or scheduled for removal.
Requests already in progress on that backend are allowed to complete normally during the grace period.
The deregistration delay is a fixed waiting window configured on the load balancer, not on the backend itself.
After the delay expires, the backend is dropped from rotation even if some work remains unfinished.
Visual Guidance: Backend box shown in three states left to right: serving, draining (fading, with two in-flight arrows still reaching it), removed.
slides.notes: Explain draining as the polite way to retire a server, contrasted with simply yanking it out mid-request. Point out this same mechanism also runs during a planned scale-down, not only after a health check failure. Exam angle: a question may ask why draining exists instead of immediate removal — the answer is avoiding broken in-flight requests.

slides.title: Sticky Sessions Versus Stateless Design
slides.body:
Sticky Vs Stateless
Subheading: Two Session Approaches
HTTP is stateless by default, so a load balancer must decide whether a returning user must land on the same backend, or whether any backend can serve them equally well.
Visual Guidance: Side-by-side diagram: left shows one user cookie-pinned to one server box; right shows the same user's requests landing on either server with a shared data store below both.
slides.notes: Tie this back to draining: a sticky user pinned to a draining backend is exactly the case that forces a remap. Note that stateless design is the preferred pattern in modern cloud architectures because it lets any instance be added, removed or replaced freely. Interview hook: ask why stateless design scales better than sticky sessions, expecting the answer that it removes the server-affinity bottleneck.
tables: A cookie set by the load balancer binds a user to one backend for the session duration
Breaks if that backend drains or fails, and skews load unevenly
Session data lives outside the server, so any healthy backend can answer any request
Needs an external store, but removal and scaling stay simple

slides.title: DNS and CDN for Internet-Scale Delivery
slides.body:
DNS And CDN
Subheading: Routing And Delivery
Load balancing spreads traffic across servers inside one location; DNS-based routing and content delivery solve the same spreading problem at internet scale, across regions and across users far from any single data centre.
DNS-based routing sends each user to the nearest or healthiest available endpoint before any connection starts.
DNS failover automatically swaps a failed address for a working one once health checks detect trouble.
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) caches copies of content at edge locations spread close to users.
Cache invalidation and origin pulls keep those edge copies accurate whenever the source content changes.
Visual Guidance: Map diagram: a user icon, a DNS resolver choosing between two regional data centres, and separately a user hitting a nearby CDN edge server linked back to one origin server.
slides.notes: Frame this as traffic steering at a wider scale than the load balancer just covered. Mention that DNS decides which region a user reaches, while the CDN decides where the content itself is stored. Flag that interviewers often ask how DNS and a CDN differ from a load balancer.

slides.title: Steering Traffic Through DNS
slides.body:
DNS Based Routing
Subheading: Steering By Resolution
The Domain Name System (DNS) normally returns one fixed address for a name; DNS-based routing instead returns a different address depending on policy, routing users to a region without the user ever knowing a choice was made.
Geographic (geo) routing returns the record of the data centre nearest the user's resolver.
Latency-based routing returns whichever region has historically responded fastest to that specific user.
Weighted routing splits DNS answers across regions by a configured traffic percentage.
Multi-value answer routing returns several healthy addresses so the client itself can pick one.
Analogy: A railway enquiry counter that sends each passenger to whichever platform has the nearest, on-time train rather than always naming the same platform — just as DNS-based routing hands each user the address of whichever regional endpoint is closest or healthiest for that user.
Visual Guidance: World map with a DNS resolver icon branching arrows to three region icons, each arrow labelled geo, latency or weighted.
slides.notes: Explain that the same name can resolve to different addresses depending on who is asking and from where. Use the enquiry-counter analogy to fix the idea before naming the four policy types. An interviewer may ask how this differs from a load balancer; the answer is that routing happens before any connection is opened.

slides.title: Detecting and Routing Around Failures
slides.body:
DNS Failover Mechanism
Subheading: Health Checked Record Swap
Routing by proximity alone cannot sense that a region has gone down, so DNS failover adds a continuous check behind the same records, withdrawing a failed address before it is ever handed to a user.
An external health checker polls each endpoint over HTTP or TCP at a short fixed interval.
A record that fails consecutive checks is marked down and removed from future DNS answers.
Remaining healthy records keep being returned, so failover completes within the record's TTL window.
Lower TTL values speed up failover but raise resolver query load, a direct trade-off.
Visual Guidance: Timeline strip: health checker pinging a region every interval, a red cross on the region after repeated failures, then the DNS answer list updating to drop it.
slides.notes: Connect this to the health checks already seen for a load balancer's targets, but note the checked unit here is an entire region's address, not one server. Point out the TTL trade-off between fast failover and resolver load as a common interview probe. Mention that time-to-live still governs how fast old cached answers expire.

slides.title: Refreshing Content From the Origin
slides.body:
Origin Pull Mechanism
Subheading: Refreshing Edge Content
Once a request reaches an edge server, it must decide whether its stored copy is still safe to serve or stale enough to fetch again from the origin, the server holding the authoritative version of the content.
A cache miss triggers an origin pull, where the edge server fetches the object fresh.
Time-to-live (TTL), set through a cache-control header, decides how long an edge copy stays valid.
A conditional request can confirm a cached copy is still fresh without re-downloading the whole object.
Static assets get long TTLs, while frequently changing pages get short or no caching at all.
Visual Guidance: Flow arrow: edge server cache box, a branch to origin server labelled origin pull on miss, and a loop back labelled TTL check on hit.
slides.notes: Build directly on the cache hit and miss idea already known, and add that the miss path is called an origin pull. Explain TTL as the timer that decides when a cached copy is treated as stale. A common exam question asks why static files use long TTLs and dynamic pages do not.

slides.title: Forcing Edge Content to Refresh
slides.body:
Cache Invalidation
Subheading: Forcing Fresh Content
Waiting for a TTL to expire can leave outdated content live for minutes or hours, so cache invalidation lets an operator remove or bypass a stale copy immediately rather than waiting out that window.
Purge invalidation explicitly removes an object from every edge location before its TTL expires.
Versioned URLs attach a new filename or query string, so old cached files are simply skipped.
An invalidation request can target one path or sweep an entire cache in a single call.
Over-invalidating raises load on the origin, since every edge must then re-fetch the content.
Visual Guidance: Two side-by-side mini-diagrams: a purge command striking a cached object, and a URL changing from style.css to style-v2.css beside an unchanged cached copy.
slides.notes: Present purge and versioning as the two practical answers to the same deployment problem: old content served after an update. The versioned-URL trick is a favourite interview question because it needs no purge call at all. Note the cost side: purging too aggressively pushes traffic back onto the origin.

slides.title: DNS Routing Against Load Balancing
slides.body:
DNS Vs Load Balancer
Subheading: Two Routing Layers
DNS-based routing and a load balancer both move traffic away from a failed target, but they act at different layers and at different speeds, which is why production systems typically use both together.
A user is first sent by DNS to a healthy region, and a load balancer inside that region then spreads the request across healthy servers, so the two layers complement rather than replace each other.
Visual Guidance: Layered diagram: top layer labelled DNS routing across three region icons, bottom layer zoomed into one region showing a load balancer fanning out to three servers.
slides.notes: Use the table to fix the layer and speed difference, since this comparison is a frequent interview question. State plainly that DNS failover is slower because of TTL caching, while a load balancer reacts within its own health-check interval. Close by noting both layers are commonly combined, not chosen between.
tables: Geo or latency routing to the nearest region
Application Load Balancer and its target group

slides.title: Building a Load-Balanced Web Tier
slides.body:
Load Balancer Build
Subheading: Task And Steps
This exercise builds a small load-balanced web tier: two web servers behind one Application Load Balancer, using the VPC and subnets created earlier. It creates billable AWS resources, so the Billing dashboard should be checked first, and all resources are deleted right after screenshots are captured.
An Application Load Balancer spans more than one Availability Zone, so the servers it balances across must sit in separate zones for true redundancy.
1. Verify the Session 5 VPC, subnets, and route table against the table above before creating anything new.
2. Add one new subnet in a second zone, plus a load balancer security group and a web server security group.
3. Launch two EC2 web servers, one per public subnet, each running a startup script.
4. Create a target group and register both web servers as its targets.
5. Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer spanning both subnets, forwarding to the target group.
6. Test the load balancer, then stop and restart a server to observe health checks.
7. Verify every component, capture screenshots, and delete all resources in dependency order.

slides.title: Confirming Setup Before Testing
slides.body:
Setup Confirmation
Subheading: Security Groups, Listener, Servers
Before testing, confirm three things: the web-server security group only trusts the load balancer, the listener forwards to the right target group, and both servers are running.
Web Server Security Group
s6-web-sg inbound rule — source is the ALB's own security group, not the public internet
Load Balancer Security Group
s6-alb-sg inbound rule — source is 0.0.0.0/0, open to all public traffic
Listener Routing
HTTP:80 listener forwards to target group s6-web-tg
Both Servers Running
Both EC2 instances (s6-web-1, s6-web-2) in Running state, ready to be registered

slides.title: Testing Distribution And Health-Check Recovery
slides.body:
Load Balancer Action
Subheading: Test And Recovery
Testing confirms two behaviours: healthy targets share traffic, and a stopped target is automatically taken out of rotation.
Both Targets Healthy
Target group summary — 2 Healthy, 0 Unhealthy, before any traffic test
Browser Test — Load Balancer Alternates Servers
Request via the ALB's DNS name — answered by s6-web-1
A later request — answered by s6-web-2; which server answers is not guaranteed to alternate strictly
After Stopping s6-web-2
Status shows Unused — “Target is in the stopped state,” not Unhealthy; Unhealthy is reserved for a running instance that fails its health check path

slides.title: Expected Result and Wrap-Up
slides.body:
Result And Cleanup
Subheading: Wrap-Up Checklist
The finished setup is a single load balancer domain name that reaches two interchangeable web servers, each able to fail and recover without any manual rerouting of traffic.
This classroom setup enables public addresses on both backend servers to keep access simple; in a production deployment, servers sitting behind an internet-facing load balancer are usually placed in private subnets instead, since the load balancer is the only component that needs to be publicly reachable.
Cleanup runs in dependency order: the load balancer is deleted first, then the target group, then the two instances, then the security groups, since each later resource still depends on the one before it.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
1. Load Balancing Basics: Purpose: availability & scalability; the single-point-of-failure problem
2. Load Balancer Types: Layer 4 (transport) vs Layer 7 (application); internal vs internet-facing
3. Distribution Algorithms: Round robin; least connections; IP hash; weighted distribution
4. Health Checks & Sessions: Health check design; draining an unhealthy backend; sticky sessions vs stateless design
5. DNS & Content Delivery: DNS-based routing & failover; CDN: edge caching, origin & cache invalidation
